blocks.text: 1. Lost-in-the-Middle Problem

blocks.alt: A context beginning and end get more attention than a context middle

blocks.text: Lost-in-the-Middle Problem covers how position within context affects a model's attention, closing out the Re-Ranking module with a subtle final consideration.
Even a well selected context can be undermined by where its pieces sit, not just which pieces were chosen.
2. Everything So Far Assumed Position Didn't Matter
Every technique covered so far, including combining compression with top-K in Context Compression, focused on which chunks and how much text to include.
Where a chunk sits within that included text also matters.
3. The Middle Of Long Context Gets Less Attention

blocks.alt: The beginning is compared against the middle, where attention drops

blocks.text: As with the context window concept covered in Deep Learning Fundamentals, models tend to attend more strongly to the beginning and end of their context.
Information placed in the middle can receive noticeably less attention.

blocks.content: {"headers":["Position in context","Typical attention received"],"rows":[["Beginning and end","Higher attention"],["Middle","Lower attention"]]}

blocks.text: 4. Why This Happens In Models

blocks.alt: Long context creates a positional attention bias

blocks.text: This pattern appears to relate to how attention mechanisms weigh different positions during training.
The exact cause remains an active area of research, but the effect is consistently observed.
5. Measuring The Effect

blocks.alt: A relevant fact placed in the middle gives a lower recall rate

blocks.text: Similar to recall as a correctness measure in ANN, researchers test this by placing a known fact at different positions and measuring recall.
Recall drops noticeably when the fact sits in the middle rather than at either end.

blocks.title: Note
blocks.content: A controlled test places the same fact at the start, middle, and end of a long context across separate runs, consistently showing the lowest recall when that fact sits in the middle.

blocks.text: 6. Placing Critical Context Strategically

blocks.alt: The most important chunk is placed at the start or end

blocks.text: Knowing this pattern, the most important chunks can be deliberately placed near the start or end of the context.
This means going beyond simply ordering chunks by their raw re-rank score alone.

blocks.title: Note
blocks.content: Placing the single highest scoring chunk first and the second highest scoring chunk last puts the two most important pieces of context in the positions most likely to receive strong model attention.

blocks.text: 7. Reordering After Top-K Selection

blocks.alt: Top-K results are reordered by importance into an optimized placement

blocks.text: As the last decision before the model, covered in Top-K Selection, top-K selection decides which chunks make it in.
A final reordering pass can then arrange those selected chunks into the best possible positions.
8. Interaction With Context Compression
As with combining compression with top-K in Context Compression, a shorter, compressed context has less of a middle to lose information in.
Compression and careful positioning both help address the same underlying problem.

blocks.content: {"headers":["Mitigation","How it helps"],"rows":[["Context compression","Shrinks the context, reducing the vulnerable middle region"],["Strategic positioning","Places critical chunks in high attention positions"]]}

blocks.text: 9. Recognizing When The Lost In The Middle Problem Deserves Active Mitigation

blocks.alt: Long context with critical facts points toward actively mitigating lost-in-the-middle

blocks.text: Long contexts with many included chunks need active position management.
Short contexts with very few chunks, by contrast, have little room for the problem to actually appear.
10. Worked Example
The example below demonstrates reordering re-ranked chunks to place the most important ones at the start and end.

code.content:
reranked_chunks = [
    {"id": "c1", "score": 0.95},
    {"id": "c2", "score": 0.88},
    {"id": "c3", "score": 0.82},
    {"id": "c4", "score": 0.79},
    {"id": "c5", "score": 0.75},
]

def position_for_attention(chunks):
    # place chunks so the highest scores land at the start and end
    sorted_chunks = sorted(chunks, key=lambda c: -c["score"])
    positioned = [None] * len(sorted_chunks)
    left, right = 0, len(sorted_chunks) - 1
    for i, chunk in enumerate(sorted_chunks):
        if i % 2 == 0:
            positioned[left] = chunk
            left += 1
        else:
            positioned[right] = chunk
            right -= 1
    return positioned

naive_order = [c["id"] for c in sorted(reranked_chunks, key=lambda c: -c["score"])]
print(f"Naive order by raw score: {naive_order}")

positioned = position_for_attention(reranked_chunks)
positioned_order = [c["id"] for c in positioned]
print(f"Positioned for attention: {positioned_order}")
print("\nNotice the top scoring chunks land at the start and end,")
print("where they are most likely to receive strong model attention.")

blocks.title: Note
blocks.content: Running this example shows the highest scoring chunks repositioned to the start and end of the sequence rather than left in raw score order.

blocks.text: 11. Common Mistakes

items: Ordering chunks purely by raw re-rank score without considering positional attention effects.
Placing the single most important chunk in the middle of a long context.
Ignoring the lost in the middle problem for pipelines with many included chunks.
Assuming compression alone solves the positional attention problem without also considering ordering.

Cross Encoder covered the most accurate but slowest technique, processing query and chunk jointly.
